transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I... I've been noticing something lately, or well, I guess my colleagues and my husband have been noticing it more than me, but I finally realized I needed to talk to someone about it. What brought me in is that I just can't seem to stay in my seat. I keep getting up. It happens all the time—in staff meetings at school, or even just at home during dinner when everyone else is perfectly fine sitting down. 

Like, just last week we had this long faculty meeting about the new curriculum standards, and the principal was right in the middle of a PowerPoint presentation. Everyone was seated, taking notes, but I just... I felt this sudden, overwhelming urge that I needed to get up. I convinced myself I needed to refill my coffee, even though my cup was still half full, or I'd get up to check a handout at the back of the room, or just walk to the back just to stand there. I tell myself I'm just stretching my legs or being proactive, but nothing is ever really urgent. And it’s not just at school; at dinner with my husband, I’ll pop up three or four times to check the oven or grab a napkin we don't even need. I just... I don't know why I can't just sit through things like a normal person anymore.
Have you had any times when you felt unusually energized or needed much less sleep than usual?

Oh, no, no, nothing like that. I mean, I definitely need my sleep. I've always been someone who needs a solid seven or eight hours, ever since I was in grad school, really. If I don't get my sleep, I am just an absolute wreck the next day, especially trying to keep up with high schoolers. Teaching tenth graders takes a lot out of you, emotionally and physically, you know? 

So by the time, say, 10 o'clock rolls around, I am perfectly ready for bed. My husband can stay up watching the late news or reading in the living room, but I'm usually out as soon as my head hits the pillow. I guess... well, I do have that restless feeling during the day, like I was telling you about with the staff meetings and the dinners, but I wouldn't call it feeling "unusually energized." It's not like I'm bursting with some kind of superpower energy where I want to go paint the living room or clean the whole house at midnight or anything like that. It’s more just this... this annoying physical antsiness when I'm supposed to be sitting still. 

But as far as needing less sleep? Absolutely not. Honestly, if I try to sit and grade history essays past 9:30 PM, my eyes just completely cross and I have to pack up my red pens and call it a night. So no, I've never had a period where I felt I could just run on three or four hours of sleep. I really, really rely on my rest to get through the school week.
Did you have similar trouble sitting still or staying in your seat when you were a child?

Well, yes, actually. Now that you mention it, it goes way, way back. I was thinking about this the other day after my husband made a comment about my pacing during a movie. Even as a little girl, my report cards—which my mother kept in this big green accordion folder, every single one from kindergarten through twelfth grade—they always had the same sort of comments. My teachers would write that I was a bright girl, very capable of doing the work, but I just could not stay in my seat. I was always up and about. 

I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was this very strict older woman who expected everyone to sit with their hands folded on their desks. And I just couldn't do it. I'd be up to sharpen my pencil, or I'd get up to look out the window, or I'd go over to the reading corner when we were supposed to be doing math worksheets. And it wasn't just staying in my seat, it was waiting my turn, too. I'd just blurt things out or jump out of line if we were waiting for the water fountain. My mother used to joke—well, she'd say it like a joke, but I think she was actually a bit exasperated—she'd say that I wore a literal path in the linoleum between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old. 

She'd tell all her friends at church about it, how I was her "little jumping bean." And it's funny, because you'd think as a teacher now myself, I'd have more sympathy for the kids who do that, but back then, it was just... it was just how I was. I'd completely forgotten about that pencil sharpener joke until you asked. But yes, it’s always been there, this inability to just stay put when I'm supposed to. I guess I just learned to mask it a bit better as I got older, or maybe it just became part of my personality, but looking back, the signs were definitely there in elementary school.
